questions.prompt: Sort each change into physical or chemical.
questions.hint: Ask each time: is a new substance formed?
questions.explain: Burning, rusting, cooking and souring make new substances. The others only change shape or state.

questions.prompt: What is the most important sign of a chemical change?
questions.explain: A new substance with new properties is the defining feature of a chemical change.
Wax melting is physical; wax vapour burning to form carbon dioxide and water is chemical.

questions.prompt: Breaking a glass bottle is a physical change even though it can't be reversed. Why?
options: Because no new substance is formed: the pieces are still glass
Actually it is a chemical change

feedback.3: Irreversible doesn't always mean chemical. Check for a new substance.

questions.explain: The pieces are still glass. Reversibility is only a clue; the test is whether a new substance forms.

questions.prompt: Which observations suggest a CHEMICAL change? Choose all that apply.
options: Heat and light are given out
The substance changes from solid to liquid
Gas bubbles appear when two substances mix
questions.explain: Solid → liquid is a change of state (physical). The others are evidence of a new substance.

questions.prompt: Match each change to the evidence that best supports your classification.

pairs.right: Same substance, only the state changed (physical)
Light, heat and smoke given out (chemical)
Sugar can be recovered by evaporation (physical)

questions.explain: Good classifications always come with evidence.

questions.text: In a physical change, no new ___ is formed. A chemical change is also called a chemical ___.
questions.explain: Chemical change = chemical reaction = new substance formed.

questions.prompt: Using the particle model, what happens in a chemical change?
options: Atoms separate and join in new ways to make new particles
questions.explain: In a reaction, atoms rearrange into new combinations, which is why a new substance forms. Atoms are never created or destroyed.
Frying, fermenting and toasting make new substances; grating, melting and grinding don't.

questions.prompt: Give TWO differences between physical and chemical changes, with one example of each.
questions.modelAnswer: 1) In a physical change no new substance forms; in a chemical change a new substance forms. 2) Physical changes are usually reversible; chemical changes usually are not. Example of a physical change: melting ice. Example of a chemical change: burning paper.
rubric: A second difference (reversibility, energy change, or new properties)
questions.explain: Always mention the new substance first. It is the key difference.
